main.text: [II, 596] [col. 54] Chapter IX.
On the Turtledove.

The turtledove is called תור thor in Hebrew and τρυγών [trygōn] in Greek. These names, however [col. 55] similar, are not derived from one another but are onomatopoeic (ὀνοματοποιητικά [onomatopoiētika]). They were formed, that is, in imitation of the song of the turtledove, which in Greek is called τρυσμὸς [trysmos], from the verb τρύζειν [tryzein], that is, to moan in the manner of a turtledove. So Pollux, book 5, ch. 14, in the section On the calls of birds: Εἴποις δ' ἂν τρυγόνας τρύζειν, περιστερὰς γογγύζειν [Eipois d' an trygonas tryzein, peristeras gongyzein]. But for Suidas and the Etymologicum, too, τρύζειν [tryzein] is ψιθυρίζειν, γογγύζειν, ἀσήμως λαλεῖν παρὰ καὶ ἡ τρυγὼν, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἀσήμως φθέγγεται καὶ γογγυστικῶς [psithyrizein, gongyzein, asēmōs lalein para kai hē trygōn, epei kai asēmōs phthengetai kai gongystikōs], to whisper, to murmur, to speak indistinctly, like the turtledove too, because it sings indistinctly and with a murmur. Hence Clement, in the fifth book of the Stromata: Γογγύζουσα ἡ τρυγὼν, μέμψεως καταλαλιὰν ἀχάριστον ἐμφαίνουσα, εἰκότως ἐξοικίζεται [Gongyzousa hē trygōn, mempseōs katalalian acharistōn emphainousa, eikotōs exoikizetai]. The murmuring turtledove, displaying the ungrateful slander of complaint, is rightly driven from the house. For others τρύζειν [tryzein] is πολυφωνεῖν, καὶ πολυλογεῖν [polyphōnein, kai polylogein], to chatter a great deal. Because τὴν τρυγόνα ἡ παροιμία ἐπὶ σκώμματι τῶν πολυλογούντων παραλαμβάνει, λαλιστέρους τῶν τρυγόνων τοιούτους καλοῦσα [tēn trygona hē paroimia epi skōmmati tōn polylogountōn paralambanei, lalisterous tōn trygonōn toioutous kalousa], the proverb uses the turtledove to mock those who chatter a great deal, calling them more talkative than turtledoves. So Eustathius, on that line of Homer, Iliad 1, verse 31:
Ὡς μή μοι τρύζητε παρήμενοι ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος, [Hōs mē moi tryzēte parēmenoi allothen allos,]

So that you may not chatter at me, sitting by, one from here, another from there. Besides the paroemiographers, the proverb is mentioned by Alexis in the Thraso in Athenaeus, book 4; by Menander in the Plocium; by Demetrius in the Sicilia in Aelian, On Animals, book 12, chapter 12; and by Clement in the first book of the Stromata. To this belongs what is said of chattering women in Theocritus' Syracusan Women:
Τρυγόνες ἐκκναισεῦντι πλατυάσδοισαι ἅπαντα, [Trygones ekknaiseunti platyasdoisai hapanta,]

Like turtledoves they deafen us, broadening their mouths on every word. Nor do I approve the proposal of a great man to read ἐκ Ναύσοιο [ek Nausoio], that is, from the island of Sicily, instead of ἐκκναισεῦντι [ekknaiseunti]. Ναῦσος [Nausos], he says, like Νᾶσος [Nasos], is a word of the Dorians and the Sicilians, who so called their Sicily. The poet therefore very wittily calls the Dorian-speaking women (τοὺς Δωριζούσας [tous Dōrizousas]), who pronounce everything with a broad mouth, τρυγόνας ἐκ [II, 597] Ναύσοιο [trygonas ek Nausoio]. This conjecture, I say, I do not approve, because there is no need to change anything, since the received reading yields a most fitting sense. Ἐκκναίειν [Ekknaiein] means to deafen the ears, like ἀποκναίειν [apoknaiein]. Pollux: Ἀποκναίων ἀηδίᾳ, κόπτων τὰ ὦτα [Apoknaiōn aēdia, koptōn ta ōta], ἀποκναίων [apoknaiōn] by his unpleasantness, or by his inanities, that is, deafening the ears. As Demosthenes wrote against Midias, p. 362: Ἀποκναίει γὰρ ἀηδίᾳ, δήπου καὶ ἀναιθησίᾳ καθ᾽ ἑκάστην τὴν ἐκκλησίαν ταῦτα λέγων· [Apoknaiei gar aēdia, dēpou kai anaithēsia kath' hekastēn tēn ekklēsian tauta legōn;] For he deafens us with his inanities and stupidity, hammering the same things in at every assembly. Thus, then, it is said of chatterboxes, Τρυγόνες ἐκκναισεῦντι [Trygones ekknaiseunti], Doric for ἐκκναίσουσι [ekknaisousi], Turtledoves (or like turtledoves) deafen the ears with their talkativeness. Among the Proverbs in Suidas there is Τρυγόνα ψάλλειν [Trygona psallein], To sing the turtledove, ἐπὶ τῶν φαύλως πραττων [epi tōn phaulōs prattōn], said of those who do something badly, because the voice of the turtledove is utterly unmusical. And perhaps this is why it is called צלצל by the Hebrews, צרצילתא by the Chaldeans, and in Arabic also صلصل [ṣalṣal], as if the name were formed from a cymbal, because it has a ringing and noisy voice. Indeed, if we believe Gesner, for this very reason a species of cicada, the cercope, is compared with the turtledove in these words of Athenaeus, book 4, ch. 4: Ἔστι δ᾽ ἡ κερκώπη ζῶον ὅμοιον τέττιγι, καὶ τρυγονίῳ· [Esti d' hē kerkōpē zōon homoion tettigi, kai trygoniō;] The cercope is an animal like a cicada and a turtledove. On these words he says: The cercope resembles the turtledove in nothing else than its noisy chatter. But Dale- [col. 56] champius conjectures that a cricket is so called from the peculiarity of the sound tri. And the great Casaubon passed over this passage unconcerned. Yet that it is corrupt is as certain as whatever is most certain, and τρυγονίῳ [trygoniō] is wrongly read for τεττιγονίῳ [tettigoniō], which is a species of cicada. Aristotle, Hist. book 5, ch. 30: Καλοῦσι δέ τινες τοὺς μὲν μεγάλους (τῶν τεττίγων) καὶ ᾄδοντας ἄχετας· τοὺς δὲ μικροὺς τεττιγόνια [Kalousi de tines tous men megalous (tōn tettigōn) kai adontas achetas; tous de mikrous tettigonia]. Hence Pliny, book 11, ch. 26: Those that sing are called achetae, and the smaller of them tettigonia. So this passage contains nothing that can be referred to the chattering of turtledoves. That chattering, though often annoying, nevertheless has something pleasing: it signals that spring and summer have come, since turtledoves do not appear in winter. Hence it is said in Cant. II, 11. 12.: For now the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. Flowers are seen on the earth. The time of song has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land. And Ierem. VIII, 7.: The turtledove and the swallow and the crane have observed the time of their coming. For the turtledove is a migratory bird ^{(1)}. Aristotle, Hist. book 8, ch. 3.

[II, 598] φάττα μὲν οὖν, καὶ περιστερὰ ἀεὶ φαίνονται· τρυγὼν δὲ τοῦ θέρους· τοῦ γὰρ χειμῶνος ἀφανίζεται· [phatta men oun, kai peristera aei phainontai; trygōn de tou therous; tou gar cheimōnos aphanizetai] The wood-pigeon and the dove are always to be seen, but the turtledove only in summer. For in winter it is not seen. And in book 8, chapter 12, denying of the wood-pigeon the very thing he had affirmed here, he writes that only doves remain all year. His words are: Ἀπαίρουσι δὲ καὶ αἱ φάτται, καὶ αἱ πελειάδες, καὶ οὐ χειμάζουσι, καὶ αἱ χελιδόνες, καὶ αἱ τρυγόνες, αἱ δὲ περιστεραὶ καταμένουσιν· [Apairousi de kai hai phattai, kai hai peleiades, kai ou cheimazousi, kai hai chelidones, kai hai trygones, hai de peristerai katamenousin] But the wood-pigeons, the rock-doves, the swallows and the turtledoves depart, and do not winter (here), but the doves remain. And in chapter 16 he teaches that it is above all characteristic of the turtledove to hide in winter. Φωλεῖ γὰρ [Phōlei gar], he says, καὶ πελαργὸς, καὶ κόττυφος, καὶ τρυγὼν, καὶ κόρυδος. καὶ ἥ γε τρυγὼν ὁμολογουμένως μάλιστα πάντων. οὐδεὶς γὰρ, ὡς εἰπεῖν, λέγεται τρυγόνα ἰδεῖν οὐδαμοῦ χειμῶνος· [kai pelargos, kai kottyphos, kai trygōn, kai korydos. kai hē ge trygōn homologoumenōs malista pantōn. oudeis gar, hōs eipein, legetai trygona idein oudamou cheimōnos] For the stork also hides, and the blackbird, and the turtledove, and the lark. But of the turtledove this is agreed most of all: for no one, I might almost say, is reported to have seen a turtledove anywhere in winter. Varro too, Rustic. book 3, ch. 5: Thrushes fly every year across the sea into Italy around the autumn equinox, and fly back to the same place at the spring equinox. And at another season turtledoves and quails in enormous numbers. And Cicero, De Finib. book 2: Turtledoves delight in running and in travel. And Gregory of Nyssa on the Song, Homily 5: Ἐν γὰρ τῇ χειμῶνι φεύγει ἡ ἀηδὼν, ναρκᾷ ἡ χελιδὼν, ἀποξενοῦται τῆς καλίας ἡ τρυγών· [En gar tē cheimōni pheugei hē aēdōn, narka hē chelidōn, apoxenoutai tēs kalias hē trygōn] For in winter the nightingale flees, the swallow grows torpid, the turtledove goes abroad from its nest. There are some, however, who think that the turtledove does not so much go away as hide. Pliny, book 10, chapter 24: More truly, the turtledove hides and loses its feathers. Others wrongly read vere [in spring]. For the turtledove does not hide in spring, but in winter. Indeed Aristotle himself, in chapter 12 cited above, does not deny that some turtledoves remain ἐν εὐηλίοις χωρίοις [en euēliois chōriois].

In Cant. I, 10. it is said to the bride in the Greek version, Τί ὡραιώθησαν σιαγόνες σου ὡς τρυγόνος; [Ti hōraiōthēsan siagones sou hōs trygonos?] and in the Vulgate, How beautiful are your cheeks become, like the turtledove's! On this passage the Greek doctors, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Philo of Carpasia, Theodoret, and the Latin ones, Justus of Urgel, Gregory the Great, Bede, Aponius, Bernard, and other men of great name, have much to say about the chastity of the turtledove and about the seat of modesty in the cheeks. But all of it is beside the point, if I may say so with their leave. For the passage is not about the turtledove there: since it has no σιαγόνες [siagones], that is, cheeks or jaws, who would believe that the bride's cheeks are compared with the cheeks of a turtledove? Ἡ δὲ ὄρνις [Hē de ornis] (says the Philosopher, De partib. animal. book 2, ch. 16)

[II, 599] ἀντὶ σιαγόνων ἔχει τὸ καλούμενον ῥύγχος [anti siagonōn echei to kaloumenon rhynchos], in place of jaws it has what they call a beak. In vain would you object that Ovid, at the death of his parrot, invites the other birds to tear their cheeks, in Amores book 2, Elegy 6:
Go, pious birds, and beat your breasts with your wings, and mark your tender cheeks with rigid claw.

For he is applying to birds ποιητικῶς [poiētikōs], and πρωσοποποιητικῶς [prōsopopoiētikōs], things that are proper to human beings in mourning. [col. 57] Accordingly the same poet, Tristia book 3, Elegy 3:
Yet forbear to tear your cheeks, and do not rend your hair.
And Tibullus book 1, Elegy 1:
Do not wound my shade, but spare your loosened hair, and spare, Delia, your tender cheeks,

And Artemidorus, Onirocritica book 1, ch. 30: Παρειὰς ἴσχνας ἔχειν, ἢ ἑλκομένας, λύπας, ἢ πένθος σημαίνει. ἴσχνας μὲν λύπας, ἑλκομένας δὲ πένθος. καὶ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς πένθεσι λωβῶνται τὰς παρειὰς οἱ ἄνθρωποι· [Pareias ischnas echein, ē helkomenas, lypas, ē penthos sēmainei. ischnas men lypas, helkomenas de penthos. kai gar en tois penthesi lōbōntai tas pareias hoi anthrōpoi] To have thin or ulcerated cheeks (in dreams) signifies sorrow and mourning: thin cheeks sorrow, ulcerated ones mourning. For in mourning people tear their cheeks. I admit that I have read in Horus, Hieroglyph. book 2, ch. 50, that the turtledove has teeth. To signify a nursing woman, and one who nourishes well, he says, (the Egyptians) τρυγόνα ζωγραφοῦσιν· αὕτη γὰρ μόνη τῶν ἄλλων πτηνῶν ὀδόντας, καὶ μασθοὺς ἔχει [trygona zōgraphousin; hautē gar monē tōn allōn ptēnōn odontas, kai masthous echei], paint a turtledove: for she alone among birds has teeth and breasts. If this were true, she would also have jaws and cheeks. But learned men have already observed that this belongs to the bat, to which alone it applies. So some change τρυγόνα [trygona] into τριγόνα [trigona], conjecturing that the bat is called by that name there, because τρίζειν [trizein, to squeak] is proper to it. Others more correctly change it into νυκτερίδα [nykterida]; and the reason why the words were interchanged is obvious. Immediately before it had said: Wishing to signify a weak man who attempts great things, νυκτερίδα ζωγραφοῦσιν [nykterida zōgraphousin], they paint a bat, which flies without feathers. And immediately after follows: To designate a man who is charmed by dancing and the pipe, τρυγόνα ζωγραφοῦσιν [trygona zōgraphousin], they paint a turtledove, which is caught by the pipe and dancing. I have rendered turtledove with Mercerus, Caussinus and others. Yet — and I am surprised this escaped them — τρυγὼν [trygōn] there is not the turtledove but the stingray, which this same writer below, in ch. 105, calls simply τρυγόνα [trygona], and others, to distinguish it, θαλαττίαν τρυγόνα [thalattian trygona], the sea turtledove. For it is not the bird, the turtledove, but ἡ θαλαττία τρυγὼν [hē thalattia trygōn], the sea turtledove, that is, the stingray, that, charmed by the pipe and dancing, is lured into the fish-trap, as Aelian relates at length, On Animals book 17, ch. 18; although Philo too refers this to the turtledove, the bird. Now, to return to where the discussion digressed: the words of the Sacred Song in Hebrew read thus: נאוו לחייך בתורים צוארך בחרוזים, Your cheeks are adorned with rows (of gems), your neck with chains. [II, 600] For this the Greeks have Τί ὡραιώθησαν σιαγόνες σου ὡς τρυγόνος, τραχηλός σου ὡς ὅρμισκοι; [Ti hōraiōthēsan siagones sou hōs trygonos, trachēlos sou hōs hormiskoi?] and Jerome: How beautiful have your cheeks become, like the turtledove's; your neck like a necklace. For, interchanging ב and כ, they read כתורים for בתורים, and כחרוזים for בחרוזים, and they took תורי for turtledoves, whereas there it means rows, namely of gems, or of golden studs. That it must be rendered so is shown by many things: 1. תורים and חרוזים are here nearly synonymous. Moreover, although the word חרוזים does not occur elsewhere in Scripture, it is very well known from the Arabic language, in which the verb خرز [kharaza] means to sew with an awl, and الخرز [al-kharaz] a necklace of gems strung together, and also the spine, whose vertebrae are as it were sewn and strung together. Accordingly the Greek renders חרוזים as ὁρμισκοὺς [hormiskous], and Jerome as necklaces, entirely correctly. 2. Immediately there follows תורי זהב נעשה לך, where it is plain that תורי are not turtledoves but a kind of golden ornament, namely chains or something similar. Hence there Jerome has: We will make you golden chains. And the Syriac ܕܕܗܒܐ ܥܢܩܐ, a golden chain. And the fifth edition στρεπτὸν χρυσίου [strepton chrysiou]; so it should be read, not στρεπτοῦ [streptou]. For στρεπτὸς [streptos] or στρεπτὸν [strepton] is used everywhere for a torque by Herodotus, Xenophon, Plutarch and others. In Symmachus, for περίβλεπτα χρυσίου [periblepta chrysiou] I would read περίπλεκτα [periplekta]. For στρέφειν [strephein], whence στρεπτὸν [strepton], and πλέκειν [plekein], whence πλεκτὸν [plekton], are nearly synonymous. Hence in Hesychius πλόκιον [plokion] is εἶδος περιδεραίου [eidos perideraiou], a kind of necklace. And the same reasoning holds for the Syriac ܥܢܩܐ for torque, for the verb ܥܢܩ means to fold and to twist. But why do the Elders render ὁμοιώματα [homoiōmata]? Did they read ציורי, that is, images, for תורי? Or did they think that תורי זהב meant likenesses of turtledoves made of gold, which was the opinion of Aben Ezra? 3. Indeed, תור with Thau here is the same as טור with Teth, a word Moses uses repeatedly for a row of gems, as in Exod. XXVIII, 17: ארבעה טורים אבן, four rows of stones. Likewise, אדם פטדת וברקת הטור האחד, sardius, topaz and emerald, the first row. 5. Nor is it obscure how cheeks are adorned with rows of gems: namely if these hang from the ears, or if they are scattered over the ribbons of the mitres, that is, the broad bands that were drawn down along the cheeks and tied under the chin. For in Syria the mitre was a woman's head-covering. Virgil in the Catalecta: [col. 58]
The Syrian tavern-hostess, her head bound with a Greek little mitre.
Juvenal, Satire 3:
Go, you who fancy a barbarian harlot with a painted mitre.
Barbarian, that is, Syrian; for there had preceded:

Long since has the Syrian Orontes flowed down into the Tiber, and brought with it its language and its manners, the slanting strings along with the piper, [II, 601] and its native timbrels too, and the girls bidden to sell themselves at the Circus.

We have spoken above about the sacrifices of turtledoves. Their chastity has also been treated, and it was proved from Aristotle, Aelian and Clement that turtledoves admit only one mate. From this arose what later writers have stated with great unanimity: that when its mate has died, the turtledove remains a widow. To this they would refer these words of the Psalmist, Psal. LXXIV, 19. Deliver not the soul of thy turtledove unto the multitude (of the enemies), that is, they say, the Church of Israel, which, even when forsaken by you, does not cleave to another God. R. Selomo: התור הזה משמת הזכר בן זוגה אינה מזדווגת לאחר אף ישראל לא התחליפוך באל אחר אף על פי שרחקתה מהם והיו כאלמנה, The female turtledove, once her male mate has died, does not pair with another. So too the Israelites have not exchanged you for another God, even though you have withdrawn from them, but have remained like a widow. But there is no need to go so far. For it is not sufficiently certain that the turtledove in widowhood does not pair with another, even though the writers who assert it
may be defended by their number and by phalanxes joined shield to shield.

But it is certain at least that the turtledove does not mate with another while its mate is alive. If the Church conforms itself to this example, it will never worship other gods, because the God whom it worships is ever living. The Israelites could also be compared with the turtledove לפי שהם חלושי הכח ונטרפים ואינם טורפים וכן ישראל, because turtledoves are weak in strength, and are torn as prey but do not prey, and so are the Israelites. This is Kimchi's conjecture. For the turtledove is a kind of dove, and the smallest of all in the dove kind. The Philosopher, Hist. book 5, ch. 13: Ἐλάχιστον δὲ τῶν τοιούτων ἡ τρυγών [Elachiston de tōn toioutōn hē trygōn]· The smallest of these is the turtledove. To the same purpose could also be referred whatever has been said of the simplicity of the dove, since the turtledove is a kind of dove. You will wonder why none of the ancient translators, as many as are extant, mentioned the turtledove in rendering this passage. For in place of the soul of thy turtledove the Greeks have ψυχὴν ἐξομολογουμένην σοι [psychēn exomologoumenēn soi], a soul confessing to thee. The Syriac and the Ethiopic follow the same. They evidently read תודך for תורך, Daleth for Resh, which are very similar letters. The printed Arabic versions have نفسا عارفة بك [nafsan ʿārifatan bika] a soul that knows thee. And one of the manuscripts in my possession has انفس يايسيك [anfus yāysīk] souls who know thee, that is, who have known thee. As if they had read נפש תדעך, a soul [col. 59] that knows thee. But Jerome has A soul instructed in thy Law. And the Chaldee version of Joseph the Blind has נפשת מאלפי אוריתך, the souls of those teaching thy Law, as though תורך alluded to the word תורה, which means Law. But these renderings are far-fetched and beside the point. And, apart from the Greeks, Jonathan, older than all of these, had rightly seen that תור here is the turtledove. His version, indeed, is not extant. But that he rendered it so is shown by these words of Selomo: [II, 602] יונתן תירגם לשון תורים ובני יונה, Jonathan rendered it as in the passages of the Law dealing with turtledoves and young doves. The Hebrews rightly follow this, as do the more recent translators, as many as there are.

notes.text: Forsskål, in Descriptio Animalium, p. 9, also lists the turtur [turtledove] among the migratory birds of Alexandria that arrive with the flooding of the Nile (that is, either toward the end of April or at the beginning of May). But he wrongly wrote the name of the animal as كمري [kmry] for قمري [qumrī]; see Golius, Lexic. Arab. p. 1964, whose feminine is قُمْرِيَّة [qumriyya]; the male is also called ساق حرّ [sāq ḥurr], on which see Bochart, preceding Chapter, p. 52, marginal note. By a strange error Hufnagel, V. S. V., in the Annotatt. in Cantic. in the Repertorium für biblische und morgenl. Litterat. vol. 10, p. 243 [II, 598] 243, note b), confuses the turtur [turtledove] with the turdus [thrush], Arab. سمرمر [smrmr], which Forsskål, p. 6 of the book cited, says arrives at Aleppo in the months of July and August. But there is no one who does not know that the turdus [thrush] is of an entirely different kind from the turtur [turtledove].
